extracted.intended_audience: researchers, journal editors, science policy audiences, and the science-interested public
extracted.subtask_description: Extract and apply criteria for judging scientific research and the incentives of high‑prestige ('luxury') journals — e.g., how research quality, citation metrics, editorial selection, replication, and incentive structures should factor into evaluation. Useful for critiquing journal culture or deciding publication/policy choices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not judge research by journal impact factor
rubrics_metrics.description: It is common, and encouraged by many journals, for research to be judged by the impact factor of the journal that publishes it. But as a journal’s score is an average, it says little about the quality of any individual piece of research.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess individual articles on their own merits rather than using the journal's impact factor as a proxy for quality. Impact factor is an aggregate metric and can misrepresent the quality of particular papers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize citations are an imperfect proxy for quality
rubrics_metrics.description: Citation is sometimes, but not always, linked to quality. A paper can become highly cited because it is good science – or because it is eye-catching, provocative or wrong.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When using citation counts, consider why a paper is cited (positive follow-up, controversy, or refutation). Combine citation metrics with qualitative assessment of methods, reproducibility, and contribution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid rewarding or privileging 'eye‑catching' or provocative work over rigor
rubrics_metrics.description: Luxury‑journal editors know this, so they accept papers that will make waves because they explore sexy subjects or make challenging claims. This influences the science that scientists do and builds bubbles in fashionable fields.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be wary of editorial selection biases that favor novelty or sensational claims; prioritize methodological soundness and incremental but important work rather than only high‑visibility topics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Support and publish replication studies
rubrics_metrics.description: Luxury journals' emphasis on novelty discourages other important work, such as replication studies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Journals and evaluators should value and publish replication and confirmation work as a core component of scientific quality and reliability, not as second‑class output.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design incentive structures that do not encourage cutting corners or fraud
rubrics_metrics.description: In extreme cases, the lure of the luxury journal can encourage the cutting of corners, and contribute to the escalating number of papers that are retracted as flawed or fraudulent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid career and reward systems that equate prestige publications with bonuses or advancement; instead incentivize transparency, reproducibility, and integrity. The page cites high‑profile retractions (e.g., cloned human embryos, contested arsenic‑in‑DNA claim) as consequences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editors and journals have responsibility to minimize promotion of unreplicable or erroneous claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Perhaps worse, it has not retracted claims that a microbe is able to use arsenic in its DNA instead of phosphorus, despite overwhelming scientific criticism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editorial policies should actively guard against publishing poorly supported extraordinary claims and should respond responsibly to valid post‑publication criticism (corrections/retractions when warranted).

rubrics_metrics.name: Decouple career rewards from publication in 'luxury' journals (oppose 'bonus culture')
rubrics_metrics.description: Schekman compares the incentives that journals such as Nature, Cell and Science offer scientists to Wall Street's bonus culture.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Academic hiring, promotion, and funding decisions should not be driven primarily by the prestige of the journal where work appears. Develop evaluation practices that focus on the intrinsic value, rigor, and reproducibility of the research.
